the role of the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway in regulating peripheral T cell tolerance and autoimmune diabetes.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

PD-L1 and its ligand PD-L2 are both expressed on hematopoietically-derived cells, such as dendritic cells and macrophages, but that the expression of PD-L2 is restricted to macro-phages and dendritic cell, whereas PD-L1 is expressed on hematopoetic and parenchymatous cells, including pancreatic beta cells.

PD-L1 has an important and unique role in mediating tissue-specific tolerance, which is not redundant with PD-L2, and that PD-L1 on parenchyma is more important than PD-L1 on hematopoietically-derived cells in preventing autoimmune diabetes.
PD-L1 has an important role in the maintenance of self-tolerance, which may be relevant for the treatment of autoimmune disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the PD-1– PD-L1 interaction in islets plays a role in the maintenance of tolerance to islets, and that this interaction is critical in protecting islets from autoimmune attack.
PD-L1 is a critical molecule that is required to prevent autoimmunity and maintain tissue tolerance.

The main takeaway from our work is that
PD-L1 on pancreatic islet cells is important for preventing autoimmune diabetes, and PD-L1 on hematopoietically derived cells (e.g. antigen presenting cells) is not.
PD-1–ligand interactions are critical in regulating peripheral tolerance to self-antigens and that PD-1 is a key regulator of autoimmune diabetes.
